newsitem.title: INDIA: Cement prices fall in north India, stocks piles up.
newsitem.headline: Cement prices fall in north India, stocks piles up.

text.p: Cement prices across northern India have fallen sharply on excess supply and poor demand, cement analysts said on Monday.

"Cement prices declined sharply by about eight to 10 rupees to 128-135 rupees per 50 kg bag last Monday in the New Delhi markets," B. Shashikanth, analyst at securities firm Peregrine Capital India said in a sector report.
Peregrine said the fall, apparently fuelled by a steep fall in cement prices in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh, was in addition to a five rupee fall during September 1996.
One analyst said the Associated Cement Companies (ACC), India's largest cement maker, cut prices in northern India last week. But company officials in Bombay could not confirm the cut.
"Cement prices have crashed in the last month and a half," Prashant Reddy, analyst at ICICI Securities and Finance Co said.
"There is hectic price undercutting, estimated at 10 to 15 rupees per bag, among manufacturers to garner elusive contracts," Reddy said in an industry report.
He attributed the fall to a severe demand-supply imbalance.
"From January-August 1996, supply has grown at 14 percent, while demand has been sluggish due to a slump in construction activity in the major metros and liquidity crunch," he said.
As a result, cement plants, warehouses and dealers had piled up large inventories.
"The severity can be gauged by the 30 percent production cutback that all cement units in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan have undertaken in September and October," the ICICI Securities report said.
Peregrine said production is estimated to have fallen by 15-20 percent in September, negating the high growth in production in the first five months of 1996/97 (April-March).
"It now appears that high sales in July was actually the result of stocking at the dealers' end in anticipation of price increases," the Peregrine report said.
"Inventories in August 1996 exceeded one million tonnes and September inventories are expected to be higher by 15-20 percent from these levels," it said.

"Earnings will be under severe pressure," the ICICI Securities report said. "Sluggish realisations, sharp cost hikes and increased financial cost will lead to significant margin contraction," it said.
It said very few companies in the north are making profits at the prevailing prices.
Peregrine expected consumption to pick up by November, providing some reprieve to producers in the next few months.
It said producers in the west are also likely to see some pressure on prices and margins. "(The) south seem to be bucking the trend -- prices continue to be buoyant," it said.
